Klaipeda Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Klaipėdos apskritis, Lithuania

Not demolished. Klaipėda — formerly Memel — was home to two figures of major significance in modern Jewish history: Rabbi Yisrael Salanter (Lipkin), founder of the Musar movement, a still-influential ethical and spiritual movement within Orthodox Judaism; and David Wolfson, the second president of the World Zionist Organization, who studied as a boy at a school for poor children established in 1879 by Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Ruelf — the school building survives today with a commemorative plaque. Jewish settlement, first recorded in the 15th century, grew dramatically after French Revolutionary ideas of equal rights reached the region, rising from 45 people in 1813 to 1,214 by 1880. This cemetery first appeared on the city map in 1840; in the postwar period it was completely demolished and its territory converted into a Soviet radio jamming station, with headstones destroyed or repurposed as antenna-tower foundations. Following Lithuanian independence in 1991, the jamming station closed, the roughly 13,000-square-meter site was fenced, and about 30 surviving memorial slab fragments were mortared into a commemorative wall; the former administrative building now houses the Klaipėda Jewish Community and an operating synagogue, alongside an alley of cedars honoring local residents who risked their lives to rescue Jews during the Holocaust.
